extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public; aspiring writers, poets, and social critics
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical-essay guidance and prescriptive observations on composing ridicule (comedy/burlesque), characterisation (especially by eyes), rhetorical effect, and the proper form and regulation of public street-cries. Combines literary-criticism rules with social/practical prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches of Ridicule: Comedy and Burlesque
rubrics_metrics.description: The two great Branches of Ridicule in Writing are Comedy and Burlesque: the first ridicules Persons by drawing them in their proper Characters, the other by drawing them quite unlike themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comedy when representing persons in their proper characters; use burlesque when setting persons contrary to expectation. This is a basic classificatory principle for writing ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of Burlesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Burlesque is therefore of two kinds; the first represents mean Persons in the Accoutrements of Heroes, the other describes great Persons acting and speaking like the basest among the People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Don Quixote (mean person in heroic trappings) and Lucian's depictions of Gods (great persons degraded). Choose the specific burlesque strategy according to the comic aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form selection for burlesque: heroic verse vs doggerel
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a Dispute among the Criticks, whether Burlesque Poetry runs best in Heroick Verse, like that of the Dispensary, or in Doggerel, like that of Hudibras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's view: where a low Character is to be raised, heroic verse is the proper measure; when a Hero is to be pulled down and degraded, it is done best in Doggerel. Hudibras as example—doggerel can be effective when degrading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor: laughter as amiable and beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metaphor of Laughing, applied to Fields and Meadows when they are in Flower, or to Trees when they are in Blossom, runs through all Languages; this shews that we naturally regard Laughter as in itself both amiable and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using this universal metaphor is rhetorically resonant; invoking mythological personifications (e.g., Venus as 'Laughter-loving') and poetical pictures (Milton's invocation) is an effective poetic strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of poetic personification and invocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's invocation (Euphrosyne/Mirth) is offered as a very poetical figure of Laughter, richly describing Mirth's company and qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ personification and extended poetic catalogue to create vivid, agreeable representations of abstract effects (e.g., laughter, mirth). The passage is given as a model to 'set down at length.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation by types of eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: Names, Colours, Qualities, and Turns of Eyes vary and often borrow titles from animals (cat, hawk, sheep) to denote particular qualities; different 'eye' types (Sun-Proof Eye, Eagle, Owl, Argus, Janus) correspond to dispositions and social behaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ocular metaphors (animal comparisons, classical types) to convey character swiftly: e.g., 'Sun-Proof Eye' for boldness, 'Owl' for sheepish dejection, 'Argus' for leering/spying, 'Janus' for double-sighted retrospection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eyes as primary vehicle of passion and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The eye is the receptacle and seat of our Passions, Appetites and Inclinations; it is the outward portal that introduces them, often expressing Love, Anger, Pride, and Avarice more directly than speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In characterization and rhetoric, prefer showing internal states through ocular behaviour: a look can convey what years of discourse cannot. This is a key device for believable, compact depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique vision and its moral/functional meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Oblique Vision, when natural, was anciently the Mark of Bewitchery and magical Fascination (a malignant ill look); when forced and affected it carries a wanton Design and, in play-houses and public places, is often an Assignation for bad Practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat oblique looks as charged signs: natural squints imply occult/malicious power; affected side-glances imply flirtation/assignation. Classify pernicious ocular uses as 'heteropticks'—improper practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social prescription against staring
rubrics_metrics.description: Staring disturbs assemblies and is not usually amendable by reason; it is a social offence greater than many punishable crimes but without legal remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical/mechanical remedy proposed: perspective-glasses (opera-glass-like) to view others without impertinent staring. Recommend public admonition and prescriptions about decent use to protect modest spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of instrumental street noise (tuning and licensing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrumental cries (brass-kettles, frying-pans, horns) are in disorder; no instrument of this nature should be used without being tuned and licensed after careful examination of how it affects citizens' ears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate official oversight: tune and license street instruments to avoid indiscriminate disturbance; limit instruments that jolt citizens (watchman's thump, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match vocal cry to the commodity (pitch, timbre, and intelligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vocal Cries are full of Incongruities and Barbarisms; sellers often use inappropriate pitch (milk cried above Ela, chimneysweepers vary between extreme bass and treble). Cries should be adapted to their respective wares and in apt phrases and agreeable sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train or supervise vendors so their cries are tuneful, mellow, and matched to the goods—avoid shrill, tooth-grating notes; ensure the voice overcomes street noise but remains pleasant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of noise to value
rubrics_metrics.description: Take care that those who have the least to sell may not make the most noise (e.g., venders of card-matches loudly outcry their little wares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce social norms or regulation preventing trivial-commodity sellers from unduly monopolising public attention through excessive noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and measure in public cries: distinguish urgency levels
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no just Time nor Measure observed: news is published with the same precipitation as fire; alarms overevery motion are excessive. There should be distinctions between spreading a Victory, a March, an Incampment, or different mails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulate tempo and urgency of cries — quick for perishable/newsworthy items but calibrated to the nature of the news. Avoid constant over-alarming (e.g., turnip-season alarms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity over idiosyncratic tune-signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Many vendors cry so as not to be understood; people know wares by tunes rather than words, causing confusion (boys buying apples from bellows-mender, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require vendors to use intelligible words/phrases, not private tunes; avoid learned, opaque cries understandable only to acquaintances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuse and adaptation of musical airs
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasant seasonal airs (e.g., the pickling-of-dill tune) are too fleeting; it is worth considering adapting the same air to other words so good melodies persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage reusing agreeable melodies across contexts to preserve public pleasure and economy of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of good criticism and fine writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and fine Writing do not consist so much in advancing new Things, as in giving Things that are known an agreeable Turn; good criticism should avoid positive dogmatism and the petty detraction common among envious, unsuccessful writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics/authors should prize elegant expression, perspicuity, and generosity (avoid envy and detraction). Do not write dogmatic, positive precepts without language, genius, or imagination; apply and express known truths freshly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical use (and conservation) of tears and feminine devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Women possess rhetorical springs such as tears and fainting-fits which are persuasive; there is an interest in understanding the anatomy and control of such 'supplies of Moisture' and whether they might be moderated or reserved for serious occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise tears and similar devices as legitimate rhetorical tools; a practitioner might aim to modulate their use so they serve generous pity, true penitence, or real sorrow rather than trivial ends.
